issues.item: Fear of Rage: I will not be able to control my anger and will do something terrible
issues.explanation: The profile is centered on witnessed trauma with triggers involving crowded places, conversation topics, and bus riding, plus appraisals of vigilance and outsider status. The anger-loss-of-control appraisal introduces a distinct perpetration/impulse-control theme that is not supported by the other selected triggers, memory, threat, or strategy items, making it clinically hard to place within the same formulation.

Avoiding sex is not well linked to the rest of the profile. There are no sexual trauma cues, intimacy-related triggers, body-related appraisals, or threat/memory items that would explain sex-specific avoidance. Relative to the rest of the selected items, this strategy appears disconnected and inconsistent with the formulation.

vignette:
Margaret, a 72-year-old North American woman who worked for decades as a network engineer and still prided herself on being composed and practical, first began to change after she witnessed a serious accident near a bus stop on her way home from work. She had been standing in the city crowd waiting to cross when a commotion broke out, people surged in every direction, and she saw a stranger collapse hard to the pavement while others shouted and backed away. The noise, the press of bodies, and the helplessness of watching from the middle of a packed sidewalk stayed with her. In the weeks afterward, crowded places became sharply intolerable: grocery stores, shopping centres, public events, and especially bus riding, where the density of strangers and the stop-and-go motion made her feel trapped and on edge. Certain conversation topics could do it too, especially anything about accidents, injury, or "what can happen out in public." When those moments hit, Margaret did not experience them as ordinary discomfort; they convinced her that the world was dangerous and that she had to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next. She had come to believe that she was permanently an outsider now, as if everyone else moved through shared spaces with an ease she no longer possessed.

Those appraisals quickly shaped how she managed herself. Margaret tried to force herself to think only positive thoughts, telling herself that she should focus on blessings, stay upbeat, and not "give the bad thing more room than it deserves." She used that strategy almost like a mental discipline, repeating it whenever the danger feeling rose. She also began avoiding the site of the event altogether, taking long detours around the area where the accident had happened, even when it added time to errands or made her husband drive out of the way. If a route required the bus or passed through a crowded commercial area, she refused it when she could. At first she told herself this was sensible caution, a way to keep steady by not dwelling on what had happened. But the more she pushed herself only toward positive thinking, the more artificial her reassurance felt, and the more she noticed how fragile it was. When a conversation at dinner turned to a local street injury, her effort to paste over the fear with upbeat thoughts only made her feel more unsettled, and the underlying belief returned with greater force: the world was dangerous, and she could not trust herself to relax. She became even more convinced that she had to stay on guard at all times, which made her scan every crowded room and every unfamiliar face for signs that something might go wrong. That watchfulness also made the triggers feel closer and harder to escape, because the more she was braced for danger, the more she detected it in the very settings she most feared.

Over the months, Margaret's world narrowed around that pattern. She still went to work, but even in the network office she found herself turning down invitations that involved public transport or busy venues, and she stopped accompanying her husband to crowded shopping centres. She would sit in the car outside instead of going inside with him. Each time she successfully avoided a crowd or the bus, the relief was immediate, and that relief confirmed for her that caution was necessary. Yet the short-term comfort fed the same conviction that had taken hold after the accident: if she needed to escape or keep herself wrapped in positive thoughts just to get through an ordinary day, then the danger must really be there. The strategy that was meant to steady her instead reinforced the sense that she was perpetually vulnerable and set apart from other people, and once that belief was in place, even ordinary public settings began to feel like potential traps. A brief mention of a collision on the radio, a dense line at the pharmacy, or the thought of walking back past the bus stop could quickly bring the whole alarm system back online. She found herself tense before leaving the house, checking exits and planning how to avoid any place where strangers might crowd her. Her husband noticed that she was less likely to join family outings, and Margaret felt ashamed that her life had become organized around not being where other people were.

She came for help after realizing that her careful routines were no longer keeping her world small enough to feel safe. The accident had been years ago, but the feeling that she was an outsider, the certainty that danger could appear anywhere, and the constant effort to think positively and steer away from crowds had never really loosened. What frightened her most now was that the next ordinary outing might become another proof that she was right to fear the world, and what she hoped for was a way to sit on a bus, walk through a crowded place, and not feel that she had to disappear from it.
